slides.title: Econometrics Course Overview

bullets.text: The course covers regression analysis starting from simple linear models up to multiple regression and violations of standard assumptions.
We study estimation methods like OLS and WLS, hypothesis testing using t and F statistics, and diagnostic checks for issues like heteroskedasticity.
Time series analysis introduces autocorrelation and how it impacts standard errors and estimation.

slides.notes: Welcome to the course overview. We will journey from basic linear models through multiple regression, and tackle real-world complications like heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation.

slides.title: Simple linear regression

bullets.text: OLS estimates minimize the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)².
The slope b₁ = Cov(x, y) / Var(x) tells us how much y changes on average when x goes up by one unit.
The residual is what is left over: the actual value minus the fitted value.

slides.notes: In simple linear regression, we fit a line by minimizing squared residuals. The slope shows the average change in y per unit change in x.

slides.title: OLS assumptions (Gauss–Markov)

bullets.text: The first assumption is that the population process is linear in parameters (MLR.1).
MLR.5 assumes homoskedasticity: Var(u | x₁, …, xₖ) = σ², meaning the error variance does not depend on the regressors.
Under MLR.1–MLR.5, OLS is BLUE: the best linear unbiased estimator.
Unbiasedness requires MLR.1–4, while homoskedasticity gives OLS maximum efficiency.

slides.notes: The Gauss-Markov assumptions establish the theoretical properties of OLS. When homoskedasticity holds along with the other assumptions, OLS is BLUE.

slides.title: Multiple regression

bullets.text: β₁ measures the effect of x₁ on y holding x₂ fixed, providing a ceteris paribus interpretation.
Omitting a relevant variable that is correlated with x₁ makes the OLS slope b₁ biased.
Omitted variable bias is quantified as Bias(b̃₁) = β₂ · δ̃₁, where δ̃₁ is the slope from regressing x₂ on x₁.

slides.notes: Multiple regression lets us hold other factors constant. Leaving out key variables that correlate with our regressors creates omitted variable bias.

slides.title: Hypothesis testing: t and F

bullets.text: The t-test statistic is the estimate divided by its standard error, compared to a t distribution with n − 2 degrees of freedom.
An F-test evaluates multiple restrictions simultaneously, such as testing H₀: β₂ = β₃ = 0 using restricted and unrestricted R².
The F-test intuition asks: if I force these coefficients to zero, how much worse does the model fit get?

slides.notes: We use t-tests for individual coefficients and F-tests for joint restrictions. The F-test checks how much worse the fit gets when parameters are set to zero.

slides.title: Dummy variables and interactions

bullets.text: An interaction term lets the effect of one variable on the outcome depend on the value of another variable.
When an intercept is included, you must use g − 1 dummy variables for g groups to avoid the dummy variable trap.
Including all g dummy variables creates perfect collinearity.

slides.notes: Dummy variables handle categorical data, but remember to omit one category to prevent perfect collinearity. Interactions let effects vary across groups.

slides.title: Heteroskedasticity

bullets.text: Heteroskedasticity occurs when the error variance depends on the regressors: Var(uᵢ | xᵢ) = σᵢ².
While OLS estimates remain unbiased, the usual standard errors are biased, invalidating t-tests, F-tests, and intervals.
We can detect it using residual plots, the Breusch-Pagan test, or the White test, and fix it using robust standard errors or WLS.

slides.notes: When error variance changes across observations, OLS standard errors fail. We use robust standard errors or weighted least squares to fix inference.

slides.title: Autocorrelation

bullets.text: Autocorrelation means that the error in the current period is correlated with the error in the previous period.
With AR(1) errors expressed as uₜ = ρuₜ₋₁ + eₜ, OLS remains unbiased but standard errors are invalid.
The Durbin–Watson statistic d ≈ 2(1 − ρ̂) helps detect autocorrelation, with values near 2 indicating no first-order autocorrelation.

slides.notes: In time series, errors can be correlated over time. This leaves OLS unbiased but invalidates standard errors, so we rely on diagnostics like Durbin-Watson.

slides.title: Key takeaways

bullets.text: OLS coefficients measure ceteris paribus partial effects when assumptions like linearity and exogeneity hold.
Variance concepts and expected values from probability underpin how we evaluate estimator efficiency and derive statistical properties.
Always check assumptions: standard errors are only valid under homoskedasticity and no autocorrelation.

slides.notes: To ace the exam, remember that OLS relies heavily on its underlying assumptions. Connect your knowledge of variance from probability to understand efficiency and robust standard errors.
